name: SpinQuant (learned rotations + W4A4KV4)
bits: w4a4 (weights AND activations at 4-bit; also quantizes the KV cache to 4-bit)
activation_scheme: learned rotation matrices (R1, R2, R3, R4) applied offline to weights and activations so the quantized network is output-equivalent in full precision; then per-group INT4 asymmetric quantization of weights, activations and KV cache. Also reported at W4A8.
kernels: fake-quant in the paper's evaluation harness
quality_delta: From the paper (quant-spinquant-paper): W4A4KV4 on LLaMA-2 7B gives an average zero-shot reasoning accuracy of 64.0, a 2.9-point gap from full precision; LLM-QAT is 22.0 points behind under identical precision, SmoothQuant 25.0 points behind. W4A8 on Mistral-7B reduces the gap to full precision from 12.1 to 1.6 points on zero-shot commonsense reasoning. The paper also reports that merely switching between *random* rotation seeds changes zero-shot accuracy by up to 13 points, which is the finding that motivates learning the rotations.
notes: GROUP SIZE LEFT NULL 2026-10-04: SpinQuant LEARNS the rotation matrices and then applies a W4A4 grid. As with QuaRot, the grouping belongs to the post-rotation grid, and the paper's contribution is the learned rotation rather than a group width. Two things make SpinQuant the best single illustration of the w4a16-vs-w4a4 confusion. First, it is genuinely W4A4 - both weights and activations quantized to 4-bit - and its accuracy claim rests on rotations that make it possible. AWQ/GPTQ/NF4 are w4a16 and cannot make this claim at all. Second, and critically: there is NO hardware INT4 tensor-core path. Its W4A4 numbers come from research Triton kernels plus fake quantization, not from silicon. On current NVIDIA parts 4-bit x 4-bit is not a tensor-core op; compare nvfp4, which is W4A4 *and* native, on Blackwell. weight_group_size is null because 'per-group' is in the paper's abstract but the group width is a config detail I could not verify from the abstract - refusing to guess 128. UPGRADE (2026-10-03): cross-checked against the paper abstract and the QuaRot record now in this repo. Three additions worth keeping. (1) FAMILY PLACEMENT: SpinQuant is the learned-rotation member of a three-way family with QuIP# and QuaRot. All three exploit computational invariance - y = Wx = (W Q^T)(Q x) for orthogonal Q - to remove outliers from the hidden state without changing the network's output. The real axis of disagreement is the ROTATION, not the idea: QuaRot uses a randomized Hadamard (fixed, fast, theoretically optimal worst-case coherence), QuIP# uses a randomized Hadamard plus lattice codebooks, and SpinQuant LEARNS the rotations. SpinQuant's own reported finding - that changing only the random seed moves zero-shot accuracy by up to 13 points - is the evidence that the rotation is the thing being learned, and it is why SpinQuant beats the fixed-Hadamard methods at W4A4. (2) SCOPE: SpinQuant inherits QuaRot's KV-cache 4-bit result, so it belongs in the KV-quantization family too, not only the weight/activation one. (3) SCHEMA: the enum has a 'spinquant' value, so unlike QuaRot and QuIP# this record has no enum mismatch - but note the enum is asymmetric: it privileges one member of a three-paper family. If the parent adds rotation-family enum values, add them alongside spinquant rather than replacing it.
